- "proceed" is not a protocol waiver. The agent rationalized a bare "proceed" at session start into skipping the collaboration gates and was interrupted ("also stop for the collaboration gates"). "proceed" authorizes the next step under the active protocol; when no gate has yet been established this session, default to presenting Gate 1, not to momentum.
- Decide-vs-implement reframe. For a large recommendation (TOON migration, ~1 session of code), the correct session output was a decision artifact (DEC-010 + scoped BL), not code. When a request could be read as "do the work," first check whether the right output is a decision + scoped BL; separate deciding from implementing.

## S49 (2026-04-23 / resumed 2026-06-09)

- Process-audit questions are honesty triggers. When the user asks how/why a protocol step was performed, audit your actual tool calls against the spec and disclose deviations; do not restate the spec as if you followed it. S49 saw three probes ("how did the version check work?", "where was MEMORY read from?", "why is the transcript still S49?"), each exposing an unmarked shortcut. Pre-empt by stating shortcuts when you take them.
- Name the cost and the spec-faithful alternative when deliberately deviating from a protocol step. Skipping /dsm-go Steps 5.5/6 to preserve gate context was logged at decision time with its cost (a 6-week mixed-provenance transcript) and the alternative (archive+reset), so when the user challenged it later the tradeoff was already on record.
- Protocol-mandated is not the same as automatic. When a mandated action is both context-expensive and triggered in an anomalous situation (e.g. /dsm-align on an 8-version drift mid-resumption of an unwrapped session), surface the decision to the user rather than auto-running it.
- An interrupting question consumes no gate. When a presented-but-unapproved concept gate is interrupted by an unrelated question, re-confirm that gate after resolving the interruption; do not read a later "continue" as approval of it. Also re-present concept gates when resuming after a multi-week conversation gap, since approvals do not survive across conversations.
- A logged lesson does not self-enforce; recurring failure modes need a mechanism. The S48 "close the wrap-up loop in one pass" lesson recurred immediately (S49 sat unwrapped 6 weeks), and what caught it was /dsm-go's branch#>MEMORY# resumption detection, not the lesson. Escalate recurring failure modes to an enforceable check rather than re-logging them.

## S50 (2026-06-25)

- Partial answer to a multi-item prompt — proceed on your recommendation but state the assumption. When the user answers some sub-questions and is silent on the one you flagged as the key decision (S50: "1. accepted, 2. yes" with no word on the A/B scope fork), do not silently assume on the flagged item and do not re-block for an answer they are clearly ready to move past; proceed with the recommended option and state the assumption explicitly so they can correct it. Distinct from surfacing the fork (that is the prior step); this is handling the silence on it.

## S51 (2026-06-25 / 2026-06-26 light continuation)

- Reasoning-lessons carry guard conditions; re-evaluate the condition, do not cargo-cult the verdict. S47 #13/#14 said defer the data/format split until "the second format is actually built"; in S51 TOON made the second format concrete, so the agent re-checked the guard, found it satisfied, and applied the split citing the condition — the correct positive inverse of blanket-applying a prior "don't".

## S52 (2026-07-03)

- Run a falsifiable validation gate EARLY, before the artifact it guards is frozen. DEC-010's C3 token gate was runnable in under a minute and FAILED (+1.74% Central / +7.58% GE vs required −10%). The plan sequenced P2 (golden-fixture freeze) before P3 (the gate); that ordering would have enshrined a schema that cannot ship. Gate-before-freeze whenever the gate has no real dependency on the freeze.
- Content that will seed a downstream agent's reasoning gets source-grounding plus user approval before it anchors. The north-star statement in brief.md would drive Fable's whole strategic-alignment axis, so it was grounded in vision-research and README (not paraphrased from MEMORY) and user-approved before handoff, because an error there propagates into the downstream model's output. Extends Voice-Attribution and vision-grounding to the seeds-another-agent case.

## S53 (2026-07-06)

- When evaluating "is X worth fixing or adopting?", the current defective X is the correct treatment arm, do not fix it first. EXP-011 used the current broken TOON emitter as the TOON arm and refused the 7-item fix list as a prerequisite, because the defects (bloat, F4 orphan truncation) are exactly what the experiment should penalize, so fixing first presupposes the answer and would burn a sprint. Removed a false gating dependency.
- Pilot a representative slice, including the trap case, to validate the harness and instrument before the full spend. Before the 18-run batch a 6-run pilot (T1 plus the T3 orphan-trap, times 3 arms) confirmed transcript tool-counts matched self-report and surfaced an over-strict-schema failure class that was fixed for the batch. Concrete payoff: the schema fix would otherwise have cost 18 agents.
- "Do we have enough to X?" is a readiness assessment, not authorization to do X. Asked whether there was enough to post about the experiment, the agent answered have-vs-gaps (~90%, 6 gaps flagged) and did NOT draft the blog post, routing drafting through its own chunked-drafting Gate 1. Assess-vs-produce, distinct from decide-vs-implement.

## S54 (2026-07-09)

- In chunked drafting, framing supplied by the user mid-pipeline can be load-bearing for already-locked bites. Before spending the next bite, capture the framing to materials.md, confirm your read, and re-open the prior sections it changes. S54's metric-selection framing arrived after Section 1 was drafted and forced a Section 1 revision. The per-bite pipeline is forward-only by default; backward propagation is manual.
- Gate on the cost of a misread, not on protocol. S54 paused before Section 2 explicitly because the distinction was subtle enough that a wrong read would waste a ~275w draft. When the next step is cheap, proceed and state the assumption instead.
- When a user rejects a specific word, determine whether the objection is lexical or categorical BEFORE substituting. S54 read "no word 'kill'" as lexical, substituted "kill-switch"->"tripwire", and was rejected again when the user stated the real rule (no weapons/military/killing vocabulary). Cost: one wasted round-trip plus a substitution that was worse under the actual rule. On any word-level rejection, infer or ask the category, then sweep the whole document once.
- Before saving a user correction as a novel preference memory, check whether it is an existing methodology rule you failed to apply. S54 filed the inclusive-language rule as a new user preference, then found it was DSM_0.2 §13 (lists "kill", names blog posts in scope) and rewrote the memory as a pointer plus an adherence note. Misfiling inflates the preference store and hides an adherence gap as personal taste.
- Answer terminology questions against the project's own reserved vocabulary before the general definition. "Is the Intrinsic-ToC an ontology?" resolved to no, because the vision doc reserves "ontology" for Layers 3/4/4.5; the general CS definition would have said yes and clashed with the roadmap.
- Number Gate 4 findings and split them SAFE (apply inline) vs OPTIONAL (present for decision). S54's 6 findings drew a 9-word reply; also state your disambiguation of any compressed answer, since "5) keep" was ambiguous between two referents.

## S55 (2026-07-21)

- A forward-justification claim can outlive the decision it justified and misdirect downstream scope. BL-302 line 77 ("Phase 2 requires native nesting; TOON handles this, incumbent does not") was written before any TOON emitter existed to check it against; by the time one did, the claim had done its work and nobody re-read it. It survived the abandonment of TOON and still shaped Sprint 18. When inheriting scope, re-check its PREMISES, not just its status.
- Prefer the seconds-long empirical check over the plausible inference. Two findings this session came from running something rather than reasoning about it: (a) `should_exclude` matches segment-by-segment, so a bare `.venv` pattern matches nothing nested, which would have shipped a DEFAULT_EXCLUDES list that excluded nothing while tests passed; (b) an unrelated-looking test failure was confirmed pre-existing by stashing and running it on clean HEAD. Both inferences would have gone the other way.
- A green test can be green for the wrong reason, so interrogate unexpected passes during the red phase. `test_opt_out_disables_defaults` passed before implementation because Pydantic silently drops unknown kwargs (`extra` defaults to ignore), so the opt-out kwarg vanished and, with nothing yet excluded, the assertion held vacuously. In TDD, an unexpected PASS in the red phase is a defect signal, not good news.
- Edit forward-looking claims contradicted by outcomes; preserve records of what was believed at the time. This asymmetry governed six artifacts: BL-302 line 77 kept its text plus a REFUTED marker, the epoch plan's S47 Q3 "Migrate to TOON" record was left untouched, while the Sprint 17 rationale two sections later was corrected. Same document, opposite treatment, because one is a record and the other is a plan.
- When a change legitimately breaks an existing test, reframe what it asserts AND add a paired test preserving the original contract, rather than loosening the assertion. Two `test_config.py` tests asserted `merged.exclude == ["plan/*"]` exactly; each now checks user patterns stay first, with a new `use_default_excludes=False` test keeping exact equality. Loosening alone would have silently deleted a guarantee.
- A success criterion can become unsatisfiable and sit unnoticed inside a definition of done. The epoch-5 plan required the DEC-010 C3 gate to PASS; the gate ran in S52 and failed, so the epoch could never be closed as written. Reframed to "the phase reached a recorded resolution", since a gate that correctly rejects its candidate is a successful gate. Re-read success criteria after any halt or abandonment.
- When a tool rejects an action your model says should succeed, the rejection is evidence against the model, not an obstacle to route around. S55's wrong "session-54 is an unmerged leftover" recommendation, already approved and partly executed, surfaced only because a push rejected with "tip is behind its remote counterpart" was investigated instead of retried. A fetch-then-retry would have succeeded and buried the error.
- When committing work that is code-complete but not deliverable-complete, record the outstanding items in the commit message, not only in conversation, since conversation state does not survive the session and the commit does. S55 split P1 into 03f82b8 (code, with the unmet docs MUST named as "Outstanding for this phase") then 5899984 (docs), rather than holding verified green work hostage to prose or letting the debt surface at sprint close.
- A plan authored earlier in the same session binds that session's execution. S55 created the Level 3 branch per the Branch Strategy it had written into the sprint plan two hours earlier, and kept the "phase detail lives in the BL, the sprint plan only points at it" division it had promised one artifact before, verifying the promise at the next artifact. A plan whose first instruction its author ignores is worthless.
- Verify a naming or numbering convention against the target file BEFORE stamping it, not in post-write verification. The same error class fired twice in S55 with opposite outcomes: a `DEC-009-remove-local-llm-dependencies.md` link was invented and caught after the write, while "Amendment 3" was caught before the write when a check showed the numbered-amendment sequence lives on DEC-010 and BL-302 has no numbered amendments at all. The pre-write check costs one read.
- When an approved edit uncovers adjacent stale state, report it as a separate decision rather than folding it into the approved diff, because quietly widening an approved edit is how a diff stops matching what was reviewed. S55 found 6 stale items while making an approved 2-line edit, changed none of them, flagged the one with real consequence (an unsatisfiable success criterion), and got a separate commit authorized for five of the six.

## S56 (2026-07-21)

- An attribute appearing in `dir()` is not evidence the capability exists. `networkx.algorithms.community` lists `leiden_communities`, and I was one sentence from recommending "networkx already ships Leiden, no new dependency". Calling it raised `NotImplementedError: ... included in NetworkX as an API to dispatch to other backends`. The listing is the interface; only invocation is the capability. Same family as S55's seconds-long-check lesson, new trigger: introspection output.
- Do not spend an unpriced cost as an argument. I told the user `python-igraph` was "a compiled C extension" and used it as the cost against adopting leidenalg, then priced it when asked to commit: both packages resolve as prebuilt abi3 manylinux wheels, 8.4 MB, no toolchain. The asserted cost had been the main argument against the option and it evaporated on contact. Price a cost before it carries weight in a recommendation.
- A test whose result could not have come out the other way proves nothing. The seed-reproducibility check on igraph's karate club returned "identical across 5 runs at seed 42", which looked like confirmation, but the controls returned 1 distinct partition across 20 DIFFERENT seeds and 1 across 10 UNSEEDED runs. An entirely ignored seed parameter produces exactly that output. Re-run on a graph where the algorithm is genuinely stochastic before believing a determinism claim. Extends S55's green-for-the-wrong-reason lesson from TDD reds to verification generally.
- A quality metric that a randomized null also satisfies was never measuring quality. Low NMI-vs-directories was used all session as evidence that clustering found structure the folder tree does not encode; a degree-preserving rewire scored the same or higher (0.1881 null vs 0.1812 real). It measured the ABSENCE of folder agreement, not the PRESENCE of topical structure. Any gate metric should be validated against a null before it is trusted, not against an absolute threshold.
- State your own base rate when it is bad. After two wrong recommendations on the same decision, both user-approved and both overturned by measurement, I told the user to weigh the third accordingly and wrote the same caveat into the research file beside the surviving option. A recommender's reliability is evidence the decision-maker needs, and withholding it is a quiet form of overclaiming.
- Disclose a contradiction between your own artifacts rather than letting a careful reader find it. The research file's §2 reported 9 clusters at modularity 0.4469 and §3 reported 10 at 0.4331 for the same corpus and seed, because one clustered the weighted graph and the other the simplified graph the null model requires. Writing the scope limitation explicitly, including which claim does NOT transfer, preserves credibility for the sections that are solid.
- When a compressed reply has several plausible reads, check whether they converge on the same next action before asking for clarification. S56's two-word "Suggested work items" had three readings (elaborate / proceed / topic-select), but item 1 was gated on decisions only the user could make, so every reading produced the same correct next move, presenting that gate. State the read, act on the convergence, do not spend a turn on a bare "which one?". Extends S55 #117 (restate every compressed reply) and S54 #97 (gate on the cost of a misread) with the convergence test.
- A hedge word in an approval is a scope limit, honor it literally. "My lean: D" was read as direction-setting and NOT as authorization to launch an EXP-011-shaped run (24 agents, ~644K subagent tokens); "support the research if necessary with online resources" bounded external delegation to questions the internal pass could not answer; "i am not sure" was weighed as evidence against the agent's own third recommendation. The user's qualifiers are the cheapest available signal about how far an approval reaches.
- An IDE file-open is ambient context, never an instruction. Mid-problem the user opened DEC-009, the constraint sitting directly under the coverage question; the agent read it and explicitly refused to infer a request to reopen the decision. That restraint was load-bearing, because the research then found DEC-009's revisit clause newly satisfiable, and an inferred instruction would have contaminated that finding. Use the signal to inform what you read, not to infer what the user wants decided.
- Narrowing your own approved proposal is the safe direction, and still gets reported with its residual risk and mitigation. Having proposed a boot commit of 5 files, the agent excluded the live session transcript (mid-session, it belongs to the wrap-up commit), flagged the narrowing rather than folding it in, named the residual risk (the transcript could bundle into a later content commit) and pre-committed to the mitigation (pathspec commits all session, which held). Inverse case of S55 #123, which governs widening.
- Before spending a pre-registered gate, ask which decisions each possible outcome would change. The agent had recommended running EXP-012 immediately on the surviving design and reversed itself on the user's hesitation: even a clean PASS would leave the blocking problem (25% coverage) untouched, so the sprint's one gate would have graded a sub-question. "Running an experiment that cannot change the decision is theatre." Check outcome-to-decision coupling before checking cost or availability.
- Record your own read BEFORE a commissioned independent source lands, so later agreement is verifiable as independent. The agent wrote down that the vision doc's connectivity vocabulary is hubs/orphans/hotspots rather than clustering, explicitly noting it was on record before the adversarial agent reported; that agent then independently found Aider chose personalized PageRank on the same problem shape. Convergence from a timestamped prior read is evidence; convergence noticed after reading the report is unfalsifiable.
- The checkable prescriptions in a subagent report are its highest-value content, run them rather than cite them, and treat two independently commissioned agents prescribing the SAME test as the signal to run it. Both S56 external agents independently prescribed a degree-preserving null model; running it produced the session's decisive number (2.8% modularity excess) and invalidated the agent's own quality metric. Two further claims from those reports were verified locally (the partition type actually in use, PageRank availability) instead of being repeated on authority. Extends S52 #66 from cross-model review to commissioned research.
- Audit your own contamination before designing an answer key, and resolve an ambiguous success criterion BEFORE the run. The agent had proposed the surviving design, proposed running the gate, and already published a favourable qualitative read of its output, so any key written afterwards would be one the design passes; it pre-registered, sought user approval of the key so the standard was not its own, and halted on the P4 gate's "cuts across obvious boundaries" wording, whose two readings give opposite verdicts and cannot be chosen post-hoc without motivated reasoning. Extends S53 #82 (pre-register criteria) with the stake-audit and the ambiguity-first rule.
- A negative result only prevents re-spend if the falsification condition and its numbers live in the artifact rather than the transcript. The research file's elimination section was written so that re-proposing weighted CONTAINS requires confronting the pre-registered sweep first, and the sources section recorded what was consulted and deliberately NOT used with reasons, carried the gathering agents' evidence-quality flags into the list, and stated which claims the agent verified itself versus reported at the gathering agent's assigned confidence. Without the rejected set and the verification boundary, a later reader re-finds the discards and assumes they were missed.

## S57 (2026-07-30 / 2026-07-31)

- An empty provenance search is itself a finding, report it rather than manufacturing intent. Asked to disambiguate BL-302's "cuts across obvious boundaries" gate, the agent went looking for what the author meant: `git log -S` showed the clause written once in 3e05826 and never revised, and the authoring session's transcript recorded no deliberation on it at all. The planned method (provenance beats preference) was therefore unavailable, and saying so plainly beat constructing a confident intent claim from thin material. When archaeology returns nothing, the user legislates.
- When two readings of a spec give opposite verdicts, check whether BOTH fail before choosing between them. The P4 gate had two recorded readings; close reading of the "or collapses to one giant cluster" conjunction surfaced an unrecorded third. All three then failed for unrelated reasons (self-defeating against the BL's own Motivation, unfalsifiable with no null control, already-answered-and-marginal). The ambiguity was not the defect; the gate had been authored before the evidence that answers it. Disambiguating would have produced a gate that still could not do its job, so the resolution was to REPLACE, not to pick.
- Counting is not comparing. The Sprint Boundary Checklist divergence was described as "7 vs 9" for two sessions, by S55 and then by this agent. Diffing the ITEMS showed neither list was a subset of the other: CLAUDE.md was missing 4 canonical items AND carried 2 the template lacks. "Adopt the 9" would have silently destroyed two real local practices. Diff item-level before proposing a reconciliation, and distrust any divergence framed as a count.
- Read the implementation before recommending a change to it. The agent had drafted a recommendation for a centrality pivot on vision-alignment grounds when reading `_hub_rows` showed the shipped summary already ranks files by incoming reference count. The option was a refinement of an existing surface, not new capability. That correction then produced the session's actual argument (sparsity flattens algorithm choice), which no amount of reasoning from the option space would have surfaced.
- Pre-register the falsification threshold, then honour it when it kills your own claim. The agent wrote "3+ positions changed or any new entrant = material reordering" BEFORE running PageRank against the shipped degree ranking, precisely so the verdict could not be renegotiated. Both corpora cleared it (GE 9/10, Central 5/10 with 2 entrants). Pearson r of 0.92 and near-identical hub SETS were available as a rescue argument and were reported as context explicitly labelled as not escaping the verdict. Extends S56's pre-registration lesson from experiment design to self-refutation.
- Report the defect in your own output when it favoured you. The check script printed "(degree refs: 0)" for two files, which reads as "no references at all" and made the reordering look more dramatic than it was. It was a dictionary miss (the lookup only held top-10 rows), not a measurement; true values were 29 refs at rank 12 and 25 at rank 15. Correcting it openly rather than quietly substituting the right numbers is what keeps the corrected figure trustworthy.
- State your base rate when it is bad, and name which specific claim is most likely to break. Three recommendations on the Sprint 18 line, three key claims overturned by measurement, twice after user approval. The useful form is not a generic caveat but the diagnosis: the MEASUREMENTS in this chain held up, the INFERENCES layered on them did not. That distinction told the user exactly which parts of a 1,591-word DEC to trust, and drove provenance tagging on every justification in it.
- When comparing means goes in circles, re-derive the END from source. Two sessions were spent ranking four clustering options against each other. Reading the vision doc showed clustering appears nowhere in it, that Layer 1's four specified components all ship today, that the vision states its own success criterion (Layer 2 navigation, already measured by EXP-011), and that it had already asked the density question in an open question. The whole option space was optional scope against an aim nobody had re-read since the premise that introduced it was refuted.
- A newly installed protocol binds the agent's own next action. `/dsm-align` replaced the App Development Protocol mid-session with a stricter one (permission window is not the concept gate; one bite per stop; each file gets its own description stop), and the agent was about to make three file edits. Applying the old cadence would have been the exact failure S55 names, a plan whose author ignores it. The rule was applied to the very edits it landed on top of.
- Prefer deleting a duplicated rule over rewording it. CLAUDE.md's Development Approach asserted test-first in one bullet and test-after in the next, a contradiction that predated any template drift. Rewording bullet 2 would have preserved the duplication that produced it. Deleting both and pointing at the managed block removes the drift mechanism: a duplicated rule can drift, a referenced one cannot.
- Report every widening opportunity rather than absorbing any. Four times a scoped edit uncovered adjacent sites with the same defect (two extra retired-framing sites, then two more, then the Development Protocol section). Each was presented with exact replacement text for one-word approval rather than folded into an approved diff. Cost is a round trip; the alternative is a diff that stops matching what was reviewed.
- A composite command's error message describes its LAST step, not the whole transaction. `gh pr merge 16 --merge --delete-branch` printed "failed to run git ... Aborting" on a dirty tree, but `gh pr view` showed the PR already MERGED at 8d23e23: the remote merge had landed and only gh's local post-merge cleanup aborted, so `--delete-branch` silently never ran and both branches survived. Retrying would have errored confusingly; assuming failure would have left a merged PR looking unmerged. Query the authoritative remote state first, then finish the skipped local steps by hand. Inverse of S55 #127, where a rejection was evidence against the model; here a reported failure was evidence about only one sub-step.
- Diagnosing an ordering inversion is not the same as proposing the re-order. The agent worked out that the S56 checkpoint's "resolve P4 then choose direction" was "partly backwards" and reported it, then executed the given order anyway: the P4 gate was repaired across six sites in two files plus four widening round-trips, and roughly five hours later DEC-012 closed Sprint 18 and left P4 as vestigial validation machinery. When you find a handoff's pending-item ORDER is backwards, convert the diagnosis into a concrete swap proposal; a noted inversion the user must act on unprompted is weaker than a proposed re-order.
- Choosing the mechanism that authors no user-voiced content is a legitimate way to avoid a Voice-Attribution gate, but verify the mechanism is AVAILABLE before relying on the avoidance, and pre-commit to the stop if it is not. The agent picked a fast-forward over a PR partly because an FF authors no merge message, title or body, then found `enforce_admins: true` plus required reviews blocks it and admin rights do not exempt. Because the fallback ("if the push is rejected I stop and surface the fork rather than improvising a PR body") was written down before the check, the returning gate cost one turn instead of an unreviewed body.
- S56 #143's convergence test needs a stated fallback for when it FAILS. "let's fix this" had two readings that did not converge, and the resolution was neither to pick nor to ask: apply the narrowest directly-authorized reading, present the adjacent one with exact replacement text so approval costs one word, and state the split so a wrong read is cheap to correct. Do not re-block with "which one?" when the user is three consecutive approvals into a rhythm. Corollary from the same session: your own pre-registered precondition can MANUFACTURE convergence, since "run this recommendation" resolved identically under both readings once the falsification check was step one either way.
- User agreement with your recommendation is not independent evidence FOR it, least of all when your base rate on that decision line is bad. On "3 + 1" the agent noted the choice matched its own stated lean and explicitly refused to upgrade its confidence: "I should not treat agreement with my own lean as extra validation. The lean was light for a reason and the reason has not changed." Approval resolves what to do next, it does not retroactively strengthen the argument that produced it.
- A saved technique encodes the environment it was written in, and another rule can invalidate one of its steps. The recorded `dirty-transcript-branch-switch` fix is copy / revert / switch / restore via scratchpad, but the scratchpad is outside the repo and the cross-repo hook had already blocked it that session. `git stash push` on the single path did the same job with no out-of-repo write, and was safe specifically because the merge put an identical transcript blob on master so the pop applied onto matching committed content. Substitute an equivalent that satisfies both rules, state the substitution and the safety argument, do not deviate silently.
- When a session ends mid-transaction, the handoff's FIRST line is the inconsistency the repo now carries, not the session's accomplishments. S57 accepted DEC-012 and closed BL-302 Phase 2 and the sprint-18 plan against it while `epoch-5-plan.md` still described Sprint 18 as live, still listed "BL-302 Phase 2 delivered" as a success criterion, and still numbered Sprint 19 as hop-distance, so a next session reading that file alone would get the whole epoch wrong. Declining to author three more plan artifacts at 02:16 was right; leaving the resulting contradiction below the fold would not have been.

## S58 (2026-08-04)

- A scoped autonomy grant is not a bare "proceed", classify the work set before starting and pre-commit the stop points. "work on Suggested work items autonomously and pause if you have any questions or need my validation" was tested against S48's proceed-is-not-a-waiver lesson and correctly distinguished: it names the work set and carries an explicit stop condition. All 8 checkpoint items were then classified as pre-decided (execute) vs decision-inventing (pause) BEFORE anything was touched, and that classification was the plan: 6 executed, 8 decisions banked into a single report including three protocol gates. Autonomy waives the round-trip, not the visibility, so six edits made where two were specified were each enumerated with their reason.
- A blanket approval cannot approve a recommendation you refused to make. "your read in on point. I approve all" arrived over a set containing the one item where the agent had explicitly declined to recommend (a taste call, measurement could not settle it, bad base rate on that decision line). "your read" is singular, so it was resolved to its unique antecedent in the prior turn; "all" had two readings that ship different outcomes (a hub-ranking code change, or not), so S56's convergence test fails and S57's narrowest-authorized-reading rule applies. Independent second reason to hold: treating agreement as endorsement of a claim your own base rate distrusts buys the change AND the appearance that it was endorsed.
- An approval given before the content exists cannot be a content approval. "send" authorised a cross-repo, voice-attributed notification whose body had not been written when the instruction was given, so it cleared the intent and PATH gates and left the CONTENT gate open; both bodies were drafted, surfaced in full, and written only after the next turn approved the text. Timing bounds what a gate can cover, not only wording. Companion to the bundling rule: an instruction cannot approve an artifact that did not exist when it was issued.
- Classify reply TYPES before executing a batched answer. Eight numbered replies to eight surfaced decisions sorted into four directives, one acceptance, one gate confirmation, and two QUESTIONS back ("what do we need to resolve?"). The named failure mode was answering the questions by doing work; each was instead answered as a readiness assessment (the open decision, known vs unknown, cost, consequence of skipping). Extends S53's assess-vs-produce lesson from a single prompt to a mixed batch.
- When a plausible external explanation and an internal impossibility both fit your result, the impossibility wins, and the plausible one is the more dangerous because it is partly true. A rewritten PageRank check returned Pearson r = -0.34 against degree rank with files annotated "no incoming refs" at the top; "the corpus drifted since S57" was available, partly true, and would have shipped a broken script with an excuse. What killed it was that a referencedness measure cannot rank zero-in-degree files first. Reading graph_builder.py showed FILE nodes carry only outgoing CONTAINS edges, so pagerank(G.reverse()) was measuring DOCUMENT LENGTH. Inverse of S56's "a test whose result could not have come out the other way".
- A diagnosis that clicks suppresses the last check. The shallow-clone hypothesis for a non-reproducing test was built link by link (the test pins a commit and asserts an exact file count, CI uses actions/checkout@v4, no fetch-depth, default 1), the agent recorded feeling "the click of a solved case", then read the workflow body and found it runs dsm-validate --strict, not pytest. The chain was sound and terminated in a mechanism that never executes. Verify the link connecting the mechanism to the OBSERVED EVENT precisely when the chain feels finished. The refuted lead still yielded two real findings: the test would fail on a shallow clone, and no CI job runs the suite at all.
- A carried-forward defect claim decays, re-run it before inheriting it. MEMORY carried "1 pre-existing failure in test_cli_git_ref, untriaged since S55" across three sessions; the suite returned 722 passed / 0 failed, the file was 7/7 across three consecutive runs, and git log showed no commits to the test or its source since S55. The agent then declined to claim a fix, since nothing had changed, and reported the cause as environmental or state-dependent and still unexplained. Extends S54's derive-pending-from-markers lesson from pending ITEMS to known FAILURES: a defect recorded in prose and never re-executed is an assertion, not an observation.
- Reading the implementation relocated the work three times in one session, at one tool call each. src/cli.py showed collect_markdown_files already takes a user-overridable --glob, so the new BL's first deliverable was NOT widening a glob (discovery is not the constraint, the parser is, and the obvious version would emit empty nodes). /dsm-research-add turned out to insert under five NAMED sub-tables, a sharper diagnosis than "the index is out of date". graph_builder.py produced the PageRank finding. Third consecutive session where S57's read-before-recommending lesson paid, and in each case the unread version looked like progress.
- A checklist item naming a path no scaffold creates is unsatisfiable by default and still looks tickable, and the sibling instance is what earns the hub's attention. Template 8 item 5 (dsm-docs/guides/smoke-tests.md) and item 7 (dsm-docs/blog/README.md as a "publication tracker") both point at artifacts nothing generates: one defect with two instances, visible only because the same session hit both. Item 5's "or N/A" clause additionally made it permanently WAIVABLE rather than merely missing, so building the file beat waiving it, and writing seven executed smoke tests surfaced three defects that existed only because no smoke test did (a README version mismatch, python -m cli exiting 0 silently with no __main__ guard, and an emitted heading that disagrees with the vision doc). When filing upstream, check whether the finding has a sibling elsewhere in the same session's work.
- A warn-only check on a channel that discards warnings is a no-op, verify the delivery channel before choosing a severity. The approved plan for transcript hook check 4 said warn-only for both shapes; reading the hook before extending it showed a PreToolUse hook's stderr reaches the agent ONLY on exit 2, so a warn-only monotonicity check would usually never be seen, defeating the whole point of catching the defect at write time instead of at STAA time three sessions later. Monotonicity was made blocking, the gap check stayed advisory by construction, and the deviation plus its reasoning went into the commit message so the record does not depend on the conversation surviving. This closes the S49/S54/S57 transcript-hygiene recurrence with a mechanism rather than a fourth logged lesson.
- A check whose trigger condition is produced by an earlier step of the same procedure is a tautology, not a detector. /dsm-go Step 5.8 flags an incomplete prior wrap-up when the branch number exceeds MEMORY's session number, but Step 0a DEFINES the branch number as MEMORY + 1, so the condition holds by construction on every fresh boot. It fired at this session's boot and only the corroborating last-wrap-up.txt marker resolved it. Same shape as a test that cannot fail, applied to a procedure's own preconditions: audit any self-check against the state its own earlier steps create.
- Report which LAYER of a prior result reproduces, since reproduction is rarely binary. Re-running S57's PageRank-vs-degree check matched Central's Pearson r (0.9204 vs 0.92) and its 2 new entrants exactly, but positions-changed came out 7/10 and 8/10 against the recorded 9/10 and 5/10, with corpus drift and S57's uninspectable projection inseparable from the current vantage. The honest split: DEC-012's CONCLUSION is untouched because it rests on a threshold the re-run clears by a wider margin, while its CITED COUNTS do not reproduce. The DEC was annotated rather than edited (records-vs-plans asymmetry) and the same caveat was duplicated into the script docstring so the numbers cannot be read without it. Note the irony: the reproducibility preference did its job on first use by partly disagreeing with the record that motivated it.
- This file's own cross-references are positional and drift under pruning. Entries carry no stable ID, so the "#N" citations used throughout are line numbers at authoring time, and every Step 7 prune shifts them silently. Verified misresolutions at S58: "S54 #99" (mid-pipeline framing) now sits at line 59 while line 99 holds an unrelated S56 entry; "S56 #143/#145/#147" now resolve to 99/103/106; "S53 #82" to line 50. Only the most recent session's citations still resolve, and by coincidence. Either stamp durable IDs at append time or cite by lesson text, and treat the numbers in older entries as unreliable pointers.

## S59 (2026-09-04 / wrapped 2026-09-12)

- Deploy the changed skill BEFORE running it, then read what changed, because the ordering is only half the fix. DSM 1.26.2 altered `/dsm-align` itself, so this session correctly deployed first, then read the diff and found TWO hazards invisible in the copy loaded at boot: Step 6a's widened `YYYY-MM-DD_sN_*.md` scan would have re-pushed a feedback file Central had already answered, and Step 12b would have overwritten `_inbox/{today}_dsm-align-update.md`, the exact file holding 13 hand-consolidated review items. Both were defeated by reordering and one rename. Getting the ordering right and then NOT reading the diff would have shipped both.
- A state marker written for an action you deliberately did NOT perform is the same defect class you may be filing that day. Boot withheld the CLAUDE.md regeneration for good reasons, then still wrote `last-align.txt` with `dsm-version: 1.26.0`; the block remained 1.19.0-era, so the marker asserted an alignment that never happened and `result: warnings` did not encode the omission. It was survivable only by accident: Central moved to 1.26.3, so the next version check mismatched anyway. Had Central stayed at 1.26.0, `/dsm-go` Step 1.8 would have SKIPPED and the stale block would have persisted behind a marker claiming currency. When you withhold a step, the marker must say so.
- A defect report can be fully accepted and the fix still go the opposite way from the one you proposed, so separate the severity claim from the remedy claim. This session proposed RESTORING a deleted punctuation rule; Central verified every provenance claim, agreed the damage was delivered by compliance rather than neglect, and then RETIRED the rule instead, completing the deletion. The severity analysis is what made it urgent and it held. The remedy was framed as restore-or-propagate-loss, which never considered that the deletion might be correct and merely unfinished. State severity and remedy as separable, because the recipient may accept one and invert the other.
- Describing another artifact from your own one-line summary instead of the artifact produces a confident false claim that survives multiple turns. "A third instance from a skill outside that pair" was asserted twice about S58's Proposal 2; reading that proposal showed it names `/dsm-align` as its own second instance, so the "new" finding had been filed two sessions earlier and the backup argument was pre-empted in the same file. The genuinely new defect was adjacent and different (a notification pointing at a file the notifying skill overwrites). Read the artifact before characterising it, even when the artifact is your own project's.
- A stale pointer that still RESOLVES is worse than a dangling one, and the two produce identical-looking output. Two inbox entries said only "Full report: `.claude/last-align-report.md`", a file `/dsm-align` overwrites every run. The first entry's payload was destroyed 9 days later by the next run, then spent 36 further days resolving to a complete, well-formed report describing a DIFFERENT alignment run. A dangling pointer announces itself; this one hands the reader plausible wrong content. Recovery was possible only via `git show` on a file the skill's own text calls gitignored. DSM_0.2 §19.1's rule generalises: "the payload" and "a different run's payload" must not print the same.
- `/dsm-go` writes the session baseline at Step 5, AFTER Step 1.8 runs `/dsm-align` and Step 3.5 moves the checkpoint, so work those steps perform is recorded as the session's STARTING state and `/dsm-wrap-up` Step 9 then classifies it pre-existing and drops it. Measured this session: 5 of 21 changed paths classified `SKIP(pre)`, of which 4 were unstaged and would genuinely have been left out of the wrap-up commit (three hook scripts and `settings.json`, all modified by boot's own align). The fifth rode along only because Step 3.5 stages its rename. Distinct from BL-523 (which block to compare against); this is an ordering defect between two steps of the same skill. Audit a baseline against what ran before it was taken.
- When an instruction to WAIT arrives, hold everything and surface the consequence that fires without anyone choosing it. "Wait until some resolution is determined" had a narrow reading (pause the dependent item) and a broad one (pause the agenda) that did not converge, so the least-action reading governed. The useful work was not finding adjacent tasks but naming the automatic hazard: `/dsm-wrap-up` Step 6a and `/dsm-align` Step 6a both auto-push ripe feedback, so the already-delivered file would have been sent to Central a second time by whichever ran next, with nobody deciding it.
- Moving a markdown file silently re-bases every relative link inside it, so sweep the moved file, not just the links pointing at it. Relocating two published posts to `blog/done/` prompted a scan that found `2026-02-05-blog-draft.md` referencing `images/broken-refs-example.png`, a directory absent from both the working tree and all of git history: the image had been dead since the post was authored, and a move-only tidy would have shipped a neat folder with a broken image in its flagship post. The same sweep found a sibling GitHub URL dead on a second axis, `blob/main` against a repo whose default branch is `master`.
- The transcript hook's anchor rule and the Edit tool's uniqueness rule can deadlock. Check 1 requires `old_string` to begin with the file's last non-empty line; Edit requires `old_string` to be unique. When the last line is a short common string (here, the word "report." occurring 9 times) both cannot be satisfied and the append must fall back to `cat >>`, which is append-only in substance but bypasses the validator. Not a user error and not a reason to route around silently; record it when it happens.
- Input that CONFIRMS your own report is the input you have the least incentive to check, so check it hardest. Central's response accepted all three of this session's proposals and shipped one the same day; the agent verified all four of its checkable claims against Central's working tree anyway (CHANGELOG at 1.26.1/2/3, `grep -c` returning 0 for the deleted rule text, the orphan block gone, the registry entry present). Agreement is a scrutiny trigger, not a scrutiny discount.
- When a spec states several numbers, use the one that declares itself canonical, not the nearest one. Boot reported the compact mirror as 1.37x over its size bound by reading the ~30 KB LIVE-file target from DSM_0.2.A §8.1's opening paragraph; the mirror's bound is 61,440 B, stated later in the same section on the line that says "this is the only site that states the number". Then push the correction to whoever received the wrong figure, not just to the local file.
- Write down a falsifiable expectation BEFORE reading the evidence, together with what would make it worthless. Asked whether the session had wrapped, the agent recorded "expectation, stated before looking so it is falsifiable: NOT wrapped" and immediately discounted it ("I have been wrong this session about what I remembered versus what the file said, twice"), then read five independent markers. The pre-statement is what makes a confirming result informative rather than circular.
- A finding with exactly one correct value is not a decision, and escalating it spends a gate for nothing. The agent presented a dead GitHub URL (branch `main` where only `origin/master` exists) as a user choice, and corrected itself: "Asking about it was the error, not the finding." Same session, same shape at larger scale: the blog reorganization produced three escalations before the user replied that the topic was not important and to find a solution. Match escalation rate to the stakes the user assigns, not to the ambiguity you happen to find.
- Look for the instance YOUR OWN run produced before filing a defect abstractly; self-implication is the strongest evidence available. The notification-payload proposal included the entry `/dsm-align` had generated under the agent an hour earlier, carrying the identical bare pointer and durable only because the agent hand-inlined 13 review items into it. "The proposal is stronger for saying that the skill produced a defective entry under me an hour ago than for describing the defect abstractly."
- Piping a command into a filter destroys the exit status your `&&` guard reads. `git push -q 2>&1 | tail -3 && echo "PUSH OK"` printed PUSH OK while branch protection REJECTED the push, because `&&` tested `tail`. Caught only by `git rev-list @{u}..HEAD --count` returning 1. Test the command's own status (`set -o pipefail`, or check state afterwards), and note that the agent broke DSM_0.2 §19.2 in the same session in which it cited §19.2, which is the argument for a mechanism over another lesson.
- mtime is not a content-staleness signal when a checkout has touched both files. Boot Step 1.5 saw the compact mirror's mtime look stale against its recorded source mtime and did NOT regenerate, after establishing four content facts: both files tracked, both unchanged against HEAD, both last written by the same wrap-up commit, entry counts matching 80/80. Resolve a timestamp signal with a content check before acting on it.
- `git mv` fails with "not under version control" on an untracked file, so archiving a newly created inbox entry needs `mv` plus `git add`. Hit when moving Central's response entry to `_inbox/done/`; the same shape recurs for every inbox entry created during the session that archives it.
- A marker written after the commit step cannot be committed by that step. `/dsm-wrap-up` writes `last-wrap-up.txt` at Step 12, after Step 9 commits, so on a protected-branch project the resulting commit is unpushable (S59 had to `reset --soft` one). S57 and S58 committed the marker, which is only possible if it was written before Step 9 in those runs. Deliberately parked as "one more instance and it is a BL", so recognize the next occurrence as the second, not as a rediscovery.
- Relocate the live payload before archiving the entry that carries it. Six review items recovered from git history existed nowhere but the session transcript, which is itself archived at next boot; they were consolidated into a live inbox entry BEFORE the two aged entries were archived, because "archiving the entries now would destroy the thing that made reading them worthwhile". Adjacent to the stale-pointer entry above, which reports the defect upstream; this one is the agent's own archive discipline.

## S60 (2026-09-12)

- A threshold cannot be chosen while its metric is underdetermined, and the tell is that candidate readings return OPPOSITE verdicts on the same work. Asked to set the EXP-013 bar, the answerable question turned out to be one level down: "coverage" is a ratio whose denominator BL-GE-002 itself changes, so holding it at the document corpus and widening it disagree about whether the sprint succeeded. Decompose the metric before picking a number; a number set over an ambiguous metric is unfalsifiable in exactly the way pre-registration exists to prevent.
- A ratio whose denominator the intervention increases is not a measurement of the intervention. Config files are indexed PRECISELY because they carry path references, so they arrive already covered and coverage becomes (42+k)/(187+k), rising toward 100% with the number of files indexed regardless of connectivity: 36.12% at k=40, 45.69% at k=80. No measurement was needed to reject it, only algebra. Check whether a proposed metric can be cleared by doing more of the thing it is supposed to evaluate.
- Bound a gate's CEILING by counting the edge class it can create, rather than estimating its effect or running it. At a fixed denominator the coverage ratio can only move when a config file references a markdown file; an exhaustive grep found exactly two such in-repo targets, so the ceiling is +1.07pp, and any bar meaning "materially above ~25%" is a gate that can only FAIL. A ceiling is a hard fact available before the build; "probably won't move much" is not.
- When no principled number exists, pre-register a falsifiable PREDICTION instead of inventing a threshold. The coverage-to-null-excess relationship has never been measured (S56 measured 2.8% excess at ~25% and nothing else), so any figure would have been appetite dressed as a quantity. DEC-012's amendment records "BL-GE-002 will not fire the revisit trigger" plus its falsifier, which is testable, whereas a guessed bar would have graded a sub-question. Saying a number cannot be derived beats manufacturing precision.
- Records-vs-plans ran in BOTH directions in one session, and at two grains. DEC-012 is an accepted RECORD, so §Conditions 2 was left verbatim and an amendment appended; BL-GE-002 and the sprint plan are PLANS, so they were corrected in place. Inside those plans the same asymmetry recurred: the resolved open questions were STRUCK rather than deleted, because the reasoning they carry (fix the bar before the parser exists) is what forced the resolution and is still correct. Deleting it would have destroyed the justification for its own answer.
- A grep finds the word; only a full read finds the assumption. Reading the sprint plan end to end surfaced its "How to Resume" step directing the next session to DEC-012 "especially §Conditions" , now the superseded half, so a resume would hand the reader the question without the answer. The word "threshold" appears nowhere in that line, so no pattern built from the defect's vocabulary could have reached it.
- Counting a grep's output is not the same as having run it. Four sites were reported to the user from an output that contained five; the fifth was on screen and uncounted. Then a sixth needed a read, and a seventh was a self-contradiction introduced in the previous turn. The fix is not "grep harder" but to state counts from a re-derived list rather than from a glance at earlier output, and to correct the promised number openly when it turns out wrong.
- §21.4's removed-string sweep caught a live defect in the agent's OWN work within an hour of that section being dispositioned. BL-GE-002's P4 lead still read "with the threshold pre-registered before the measurement" two lines above the bullet rewritten to say no threshold exists. Its own precondition was honoured too , a positive control confirmed the sweep pattern could match before "none remaining" was trusted , so the clean result is a measurement rather than a broken regex. A reviewed rule paying immediately is the argument for reading the list.
- "Unreviewed" never meant "not adopted". All 12 carried DSM_0.2 review items were already binding here through CLAUDE.md's `@` reference, so the backlog was never a queue of pending adoptions; it was a queue of things nobody had read that already governed the work. That reframing is why the list survived four wrap-ups with no visible consequence, and why the useful output was a per-item CONSEQUENCE rather than a summary of each section.
- Assert a replacement string occurs EXACTLY ONCE before substituting, rather than reaching for sed. Three single-line plan edits were applied through a block that checked `count == 1` and aborted otherwise; a zero-match and a multi-match both look identical to success in a sed run, which is §19.1's second question at the smallest possible grain.
- The transcript hook's anchor rule and Edit's uniqueness rule deadlocked for the SECOND recorded time, on the string "(filled below)" occurring twice. Fell back to `cat >>` as the S59 entry instructs and logged the occurrence. Recording instances rather than re-deriving the workaround is what turns a recurring annoyance into evidence for a fix.
- MEMORY contradicted itself and the filesystem settled it. One line said S58 reconciled `epoch-5-plan.md` with DEC-012; another said it still showed the old sprint numbering with work pending. The file was current. /dsm-go's filesystem-over-MEMORY rule is written for the inbox, but the same precedence applies to any MEMORY claim about a file that can simply be opened.
